sections.title: People & Politics
sections.description: Important developments in governments, societies and the people shaping the world.

cards.title: Router glitch grounds US air traffic, highlighting FAA's contractor concerns
cards.content: A recent nationwide ground stop of air traffic in the US was triggered by a router installed by a private contractor, L3Harris, at a remote FAA facility in Arkansas. According to sources, the contractor's work was not closely monitored by the FAA technician present at the site, despite the agency's claim that the technician was overseeing the upgrade. The dispute highlights concerns over the FAA's modernization process and the role of private contractors in maintaining the nation's air traffic control system. The agency's policy change in 2025, which shifted from requesting maintenance to receiving notifications, has led to less oversight and potentially increased risks. The incident underscores the complexities of a system operated by the federal government yet owned by private companies.

cards.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Resigns Amid Scandal, Casting AI Uncertainty
cards.content: The CEO of US microchip manufacturer Nvidia, Jensen Huang, has resigned following revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with a Chinese spy. This has sparked concerns about the future direction of the company, which is a major player in the artificial intelligence (AI) industry. Nvidia's rapid growth has been driven by its dominance in the AI chip market, and its quarterly sales have doubled from a year earlier. The company's strategy and spending plans are now uncertain, and there is a risk that Nvidia could change its strategy and rein in spending, which could have a knock-on effect on the wider AI industry and the economy. Some investors are worried about the potential impact of Nvidia's departure from the AI market, particularly given the company's use of 'circular financing' to provide funds to its customers and other firms in the supply chain.

sections.title: Science and technology
sections.description: Discover breakthroughs in science, space, computing and emerging technology.

cards.title: Scientists reveal narwhal tusk's unique spiral structure
cards.content: Scientists have made a groundbreaking discovery about the internal structure of narwhal tusks, revealing two intertwined spirals that twist in opposite directions. This unique structure helps the enormous tooth withstand mechanical stress and provides a new explanation for the anatomy behind one of nature's most recognizable features. The findings, published in Nature Communications, offer a new perspective on the narwhal's tusk, which has fascinated scientists for years. The study also investigates how the tusk grows and how it can preserve a record of the Arctic environment over decades. The research team used a specialized X-ray technique to examine the microscopic building blocks of the tusk, and their findings provide new insights into the remarkable properties of the narwhal's tooth.

cards.title: IEA warns data center power demand may double by 2030
cards.content: The International Energy Agency warned that the global electricity use by data centers could double by 2030, potentially straining power grids and delaying new projects. The agency forecasts that data centers will consume around 1,000 terawatt-hours of electricity a year by 2030, citing large project pipelines in several regions. If grid upgrades are not made, power networks could become less reliable, and new projects may face longer waits to connect. The agency also projects that peak electricity demand will rise 40% to 50% by 2035, and grid spending is expected to rise 75% over the next decade. The IEA emphasized the importance of reliable power grids as countries seek to reduce their reliance on imported oil and gas through electrification.

cards.title: Estonian Tech Billionaire Jaan Tallinn to Gain Billions in Anthropic IPO
cards.content: Jaan Tallinn, an Estonian tech billionaire and AI safety advocate, is set to be one of the biggest winners in Anthropic's upcoming IPO, with his initial investment potentially returning tens of billions. Tallinn co-founded Skype and led Anthropic's first funding round, five years ago, before the company's Claude chatbot became a market success. Anthropic's IPO, set to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT, is expected to be the largest in history, valuing the company at around $1.4 trillion. Tallinn's exact return will depend on the level of dilution in subsequent funding rounds and whether he sold any shares. Despite his concerns about AI's existential risk, Tallinn's investment in Anthropic has paid off, and he will benefit from the company's commercial success, which some worry may come at the expense of AI safety.

sections.title: Health & wellness
sections.description: Medical research, public health and discoveries that affect everyday wellbeing.

cards.title: Texas A&M Study Finds Hormone Linked to Heart Trouble Promotes Blood Clots
cards.content: Researchers at Texas A&M University have discovered that a hormone used to detect heart trouble, called B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP), can also promote dangerous blood clots in experiments. This finding suggests a possible way to prevent blockages without disrupting normal healing. Heart disease remains the leading cause of death in the United States, claiming a life nearly every 34 seconds. The study, published in Blood, identifies a molecular pathway that could eventually offer a more targeted way to prevent dangerous blood clots. The researchers found that elevated BNP can directly activate blood platelets and accelerate clot formation, which can obstruct circulation and trigger life-threatening events such as heart attacks and pulmonary embolisms. The discovery emerged from years of work examining platelet activity and cardiovascular disease, and could have implications for how dangerous blood clots are prevented. Existing antiplatelet medications reduce the ability of platelets to form clots, but their effects throughout the body can increase the risk of serious internal bleeding. By targeting the interaction between BNP and NPRA, researchers hope to develop treatments that interfere with harmful clot formation while preserving the normal clotting needed to heal injuries.

cards.title: Drug Breaks Down Tumor Barrier, Eliminates Cancer in Mice
cards.content: Researchers have developed an experimental drug that can help the immune system attack and eliminate cancerous tumors, even if they have previously resisted treatment. The drug, called FEBP-sTβRII, works by breaking down a protective barrier that many tumors create to keep the immune system out. In a study published in Cancer Cell, the drug was tested on mice and was found to eliminate aggressive pancreatic tumors, prevent breast cancer from spreading, and provide lasting immune protection against future cancers. The study's lead author, Dr. Seong-Jin Kim, believes that this approach has the potential to reach beyond a single cancer and provide protection against other types of cancer as well.

sections.title: Environment
sections.description: Climate, oceans, ecosystems and the changing planet around us.

cards.title: Ministers Urge COP31 to Advance Fossil Fuel Transition
cards.content: In a significant move, over 10 ministers have urged the presidencies of the 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) to advance roadmaps for transitioning away from fossil fuels. This follows announcements from Denmark, Luxembourg, Spain, and Portugal of new national plans. Meanwhile, developing nations are demanding greater financial support for a fair transition. The UN climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, is seeing growing political support for turning last year's COP28 commitment into national action plans. However, negotiations at COP31 have exposed divisions over how to implement the commitment, including concerns over international roadmaps constraining national energy policies and financing for developing countries.

cards.title: Human metabolism's carbon dioxide emissions rise 74% in 30 years
cards.content: A new study by the University of Bath has found that the amount of carbon dioxide produced by human metabolism has increased by 74% over the past three decades, with the global total reaching an estimated 2.05 billion metric tons annually by 2015. The study, published in The Lancet Planetary Health, analyzed thousands of real-world measurements of CO2 production in people of all ages and found that the increase is mainly due to population growth, with more than 60% of the rise attributed to an increase in the number of people rather than a significant change in the amount produced by each individual. The researchers suggest that accounting for this activity could help scientists more accurately predict how effective carbon reduction strategies may be.

cards.title: Srinagar's Water Crisis Worsens due to Climate Change
cards.content: In Srinagar, a water crisis has been ongoing for years, causing daily struggles for residents like Mehak and Zamrood. The absence of a regular water supply has led to the installation of tanks and a hand pump at their homes. Climate change is affecting Doodh Ganga, a vital source of drinking water, causing erratic water supply, low flow, and dry taps. The river's water availability is decreasing due to rising temperatures, changing rainfall patterns, and declining snowmelt. The Kashmir Valley's 24 watersheds, including Doodh Ganga, are experiencing similar impacts.

sections.title: Entertainment
sections.description: Stories from film, music, sports, culture and the world of entertainment.

cards.title: UK gives latest Grand Theft Auto 18+ rating
cards.content: The latest Grand Theft Auto game has been assigned an 18+ rating by the Games Rating Authority (GRA) in the UK. To decide, examiners like Sadie West play the game, analyzing its content, including violence, gore, and language, to ensure it's suitable for adults only. West, a lifelong gamer, uses her controller skills to explore different choices and scenarios, playing the game several days to cover all aspects. After completing her analysis, she writes a report, which is kept on record and shared online, following strict classification criteria overseen by a panel of child welfare experts and psychologists.

cards.title: Antiques dealer's unusual gates stun Harry Potter set designer
cards.content: An antiques dealer named Joel Paxton, who runs Rustique Living in Sandon, Staffordshire, unexpectedly gained attention online when he posted a video of a set of gates on social media. The video, which received nearly 950,000 views on Facebook, attracted negative comments from some viewers, but also caught the attention of a set designer working on the new Harry Potter TV series. The set designer contacted Paxton, and he was given a behind-the-scenes glimpse of the production. This is not the first time Rustique Living has supplied items to TV and film productions; they have also worked on shows like The Traitors. Paxton started his business during the Covid pandemic while studying for a business degree at Keele University, and it has since grown into a shop specializing in unusual antiques and furniture.

cards.title: Westside Cowboy wins BBC Introducing Artist of the Year 2026
cards.content: The Westside Cowboy band, formed in Manchester in 2023, has been announced as the BBC Introducing Artist of the Year 2026. The band, consisting of Jimmy Bradbury, Reuben Haycocks, Aoife Anson O'Connell, and Paddy Murphy, started out playing in various local pubs before gaining popularity after uploading their debut single to the BBC Introducing platform in 2024. They have since released their second single, Shells, and have played at the BBC Introducing stage at Glastonbury Festival. Their debut album, It Goes On, was released in August and peaked at number five in the UK charts. The band expressed gratitude to the BBC Introducing network and listeners for their support, stating that the award is a surreal recognition of their music.

sections.title: economy
sections.description: Markets, businesses, trade and economic changes shaping the global economy.

cards.title: Airbnb Limits Host Rules, Guests' Chores
cards.content: Airbnb has introduced new rules for hosts, limiting what they can reasonably ask guests to do. The rules, announced last month, allow hosts to set seven standard house rules, including limits on overnight guests, pets, and smoking. They cannot, however, ask guests to do chores like washing up, removing sheets, or taking out the trash. Hosts can appeal to Airbnb if they have a compelling reason to have an additional rule. The changes aim to make house rules 'clearer' and increase bookings, but some hosts may have to pass on extra cleaning costs to guests. Guests like Jessica Newhook have welcomed the changes, finding lengthy checkout lists and hefty cleaning fees frustrating. The new rules have added to growing frustration among owners following Airbnb's commission rate increases last year, leading some to invest in their own websites and social media to attract direct bookings.

cards.title: AI-Enhanced Images Raise Concerns of Misleading Homebuyers
cards.content: Estate agents are increasingly using AI to enhance property images, making homes seem more appealing. However, this practice, dubbed 'housefishing', has raised concerns among experts and homebuyers that it can mislead and waste time. Olivia Nicole, 29, was shocked to find that a five-bedroom property she viewed had been significantly altered from its online listing, with smaller rooms, different decor, and structural features changed. The AI-enhanced images, used on Rightmove, Zoopla, and Winkworth, were not clearly labeled as such, leading Olivia to feel her time was wasted. Experts warn that estate agents must use AI responsibly, labeling enhanced images and avoiding structural changes that can mislead consumers. As the trend continues to grow, concerns are rising that AI-enhanced images may become more widespread, potentially leading to more instances of 'housefishing'.

cards.title: Nscale to Build UK's Largest AI Data Centre in Loughton, Despite Microsoft Pullout
cards.content: Nscale, a tech company, has reaffirmed its plans to build the UK's largest AI data centre in Loughton, Essex, despite Microsoft's decision to pull out of the project. Microsoft had agreed to fund a supercomputer at the site, but its involvement has been terminated. Nscale is exploring alternative power sources and maintaining a strong relationship with Microsoft for other projects globally. The data centre was expected to receive its power supply by the end of this year, but this has been delayed until the 2030s due to a London-wide grid issue. The project is expected to create 250 permanent jobs when it opens.
